svg.title: Exchange surfaces
svg.desc: WHY EXCHANGE SYSTEMS?: A single-celled organism has a large surface area to volume ratio → exchange across its outer surface can meet its needs. Large multicellular organisms have lower SA:V and long diffusion distances. They need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems to deliver and remove enough substances. SURFACE AREA TO VOLUME: For a cube of side a: surface area = 6a²; volume = a³. 1 cm cube: 6 cm² ÷ 1 cm³ → 6:1. 3 cm cube: 54 cm² ÷ 27 cm³ → 2:1. The larger cube has more total surface area, but less surface per unit volume. Splitting a solid into small pieces exposes more area without changing its total volume. LUNG ALVEOLI: Many tiny air sacs → large surface area. Thin alveolar and capillary walls → short diffusion path. Good blood supply and ventilation maintain steep gradients. Oxygen: alveolar air → blood. Carbon dioxide: blood → alveolar air. An alveolus is an air sac, not a whole lung. SMALL INTESTINE: Villi and microvilli → large absorption surface area. Thin lining → short diffusion distance. Good blood supply carries absorbed substances away → maintains gradients. Sugars can enter the blood by active transport even against a concentration gradient. Connect each adaptation to its effect. FISH GILLS: Many filaments and lamellae → large area. Thin surfaces → short diffusion distance. Good blood supply carries substances to and from the surface. Water flow maintains gradients for gas exchange. Oxygen diffuses from water into blood; carbon dioxide moves out. PLANT ROOTS: Root hairs give a large contact area with the soil. Water enters by osmosis, across a partially permeable membrane. Mineral ions can enter by active transport against their concentration gradient. Respiration supplies the energy for active transport. PLANT LEAVES: Broad → large area for exchange. Thin → short diffusion distance. Stomata allow gases to enter and leave. Internal air spaces shorten gas diffusion paths. Carbon dioxide enters for photosynthesis; oxygen can diffuse out. State the substance and its direction in context. THE FOUR USEFUL ADAPTATIONS: Large area → more particles cross at once. Thin barrier → shorter diffusion path. Efficient blood supply → brings or removes substances to maintain gradients. Ventilation → refreshes air or water at gas-exchange surfaces. Use adaptation → effect → faster exchange in explanations.

svg.text: Many thin lamellae → large exchange area
